draft.title: Critical elements
card: A critical element is one that industry and society need but that is scarce or hard to get. Supply can be limited by small deposits, by mining in only a few places, or by how hard it is to extract.
Helium is used to cool the magnets in MRI scanners. Phosphorus is used in fertiliser, and farming needs it to grow crops. Rare-earth metals are used in magnets, phone screens and wind turbines.
Many of these elements cannot be made by chemical reactions. Once they are lost, they are hard to replace. Helium, for example, escapes into the atmosphere when a gas is released.
Recycling recovers these elements from waste, such as old electronics. This makes supply last longer, and it reduces the need to mine new ore.
draft.remember: Critical elements are needed but scarce, so recovering them by recycling helps supply last.

a.q: Why is a rare-earth metal called a critical element?
opts: It is needed for technology but its supply is limited
It is the most common metal in Earth's crust
It can be made easily in a reaction when stocks run low
It is only used in one product, so it is not needed
a.why: A critical element is needed by industry and is scarce or hard to get. The rare-earth metals fit this because they are used in magnets and screens but supply is limited. They are not common, and they cannot be made simply by a chemical reaction.
a.clue: Think about need and supply together.

b.q: Dev runs a recycling plant in Geelong. He starts recovering rare-earth metals from old phones. Why does this help the supply of these elements?
opts: It reuses limited atoms, so less new ore is needed
It turns common elements into rare-earth metals
It makes the rare-earth metals less useful to industry
It makes more atoms of these elements as they are recycled
b.why: Recycling recovers atoms that are already in use, so less new ore needs to be mined. The atoms are not created by recycling, and common elements are not turned into rare ones by a chemical reaction. The tempting option is that recycling makes more atoms, but it only recovers those that exist.
b.clue: Recycling gets back atoms that already exist.

a.best: It is needed for technology but its supply is limited

b.best: It reuses limited atoms, so less new ore is needed

problems.detail: "Many of these elements cannot be made by chemical reactions" implies some elements can be made by chemical reactions. No element can be made by a chemical reaction. It should say these elements, like all elements, cannot be made by chemical reactions.

Why (a) says rare-earth metals "cannot be made simply by a chemical reaction", which suggests a more complex reaction could make them. It also says flatly that they "are not common". Several rare-earth metals are about as abundant in the crust as common metals. Their supply is limited because concentrated deposits are few and extraction is hard, which is how the card puts it. (This concerns why (a); the part is listed as b only because the field was mis-set.)

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The card wrongly implies that some elements can be made by chemical reactions ("Many of these elements cannot be made"). Why (a) repeats this with "simply" and overstates rare-earth scarcity as "not common".
